lines.speaker: Antilochus
lines.text: Achilles, what you were saying to Odysseus the other day about death—honestly, it was shabby. Unworthy of both your tutors, Chiron and Phoenix. I was listening when you said you would rather be alive as a hired hand in the fields, working for some landless nobody with barely enough to live on, than rule over all the dead.

lines.speaker: Antilochus
lines.text: That is the sort of thing you might expect from some cowardly Phrygian, someone absurdly attached to being alive. But the son of Peleus? The most danger-loving of all the heroes? To think so meanly of yourself is a disgrace, and it flatly contradicts the life you actually lived. You could have ruled in Phthia for years, quietly and without glory. Instead, you chose death with a fine reputation attached.

lines.speaker: Achilles
lines.text: Son of Nestor, back then I had no experience of this place. I did not know which was really better. So I chose that miserable little scrap of fame over life. Now I understand: fame is useless, even if the people upstairs recite it at full volume.

lines.speaker: Achilles
lines.text: Among the dead, everyone has the same rank. That beauty of mine, Antilochus, is gone. So is the strength. We all lie under the same darkness, all alike, not different from one another in the least. The Trojan dead do not fear me; the Achaeans do not court me. There is perfect equality of speech here, and dead is dead—bad man, good man, same condition. That is what hurts. I am sick with it: I am not alive, even as a laborer.

lines.speaker: Antilochus
lines.text: Still—what is anyone supposed to do, Achilles? Nature settled this: everybody dies. So we have to abide by the rule and not torment ourselves over what has been assigned.

lines.speaker: Antilochus
lines.text: Besides, look how many of your friends are here around you. Odysseus will certainly arrive before long too. There is some comfort in the fact that the thing is shared—that you are not the only one it has happened to. Look at Heracles, Meleager, all those remarkable men. I doubt any of them would agree to go back up if the offer were to be sent back as hired hands to landless paupers.

lines.speaker: Achilles
lines.text: That is friendly advice. But somehow the memory of life keeps hurting me. I suspect it hurts each of you too. And if you will not admit it, that only makes you worse off—you suffer it privately and call that dignity.

lines.speaker: Antilochus
lines.text: No, Achilles. Better off. We can see that talking about it does no good. So we have decided to keep quiet, carry it, and endure it—if only to avoid getting laughed at, the way you do, wishing out loud for arrangements like that.
